text: Octavia E. Butler chose low-demand jobs on purpose so she could get up at two or three in the morning to write before work.
checked: Early life and career section: undemanding jobs let her rise at two or three a.m. to write; series of temporary jobs.

text: Octavia E. Butler sold her first stories at the Clarion workshop, then faced five more years of rejection slips before she sold another word. She kept going and later became the first science fiction writer to win a MacArthur Fellowship.
checked: Career section: Clarion sales, her recollection of five more years of rejection slips, 1995 MacArthur as first SF writer.

text: Toni Morrison was 39 when her first novel, The Bluest Eye, came out in 1970. She liked to write in the early morning, making coffee while it was still dark and starting as the sun came up.
checked: Published in 1970 when she was 39; early-morning routine with coffee before sunrise.

text: Stephen King gave up on an early draft of Carrie and threw the pages away. His wife, Tabitha, pulled them out of the trash and urged him to keep going.
checked: Item 1: King threw away the Carrie draft; Tabitha retrieved it and encouraged him.

text: As the story goes, Harper Lee got so frustrated with To Kill a Mockingbird that she tossed the manuscript out a window into the snow. She called her editor, Tay Hohoff, who told her to go outside and pick up the pages. The book came out in 1960 and won the Pulitzer Prize.
checked: Per Shields biography as cited: Lee threw the manuscript out the window into the snow, called Hohoff in tears, and was told to go pick up the pages. Published 1960; Pulitzer 1961.

text: Anthony Trollope started writing at 5:30 every morning and wrote for three hours before his day job at the Post Office. He paced himself with a watch, aiming for 250 words every 15 minutes, and finished 47 novels.
checked: Began at 5.30 each morning, three hours before Post Office job, 250 words per 15 minutes with a watch, 47 novels.

text: Maya Angelou kept a hotel room just for writing, renting it for a few months at a time. She left home at six, tried to be at work by six thirty, and asked that everything be taken off the walls.
checked: Paris Review Art of Fiction No. 119: rents a hotel room for a few months, leaves home at six, at work by six-thirty, everything taken off the walls.

text: Walter Mosley started writing at 34 while working as a computer programmer. He took a writing course at City College in Harlem, and his first novel, Devil in a Blue Dress, came out in 1990.
checked: Started writing at 34; programming computers; writing course at City College; Devil in a Blue Dress, 1990.

text: Haruki Murakami decided to write a novel while watching a baseball game in 1978. He was running a jazz bar at the time, so he wrote late at night at his kitchen table, and the first draft took about six months.
checked: April 1978 Jingu Stadium moment; ran a jazz bar; wrote late at night at the kitchen table; Hear the Wind Sing over about six months.

text: To find his first style, Haruki Murakami typed the opening of his debut novel in English, which forced him into short, simple sentences. Then he rewrote it in Japanese by hand.
checked: Switched to an Olivetti typewriter, wrote the opening in English, then rendered it back into Japanese with a fountain pen.

text: Ray Bradbury wrote the first version of Fahrenheit 451 on a rented typewriter in the basement of the UCLA library. The machines cost ten cents per half hour, and the whole draft took nine days and $9.80 in dimes.
checked: UCLA library basement typing room; 10 cents per half hour; 25,000-word version in nine days; dimes totalled $9.80.

text: Agatha Christie wrote her first novel on a dare from her sister while volunteering in a hospital dispensary during World War I. Six publishers turned it down before it was accepted.
checked: Dare from sister Madge; begun while volunteering in Torquay hospital dispensary in WWI; rejected by six publishers.

text: Anthony Trollope wrote dozens of novels and also helped bring the pillar box, the freestanding street post box, to Britain. The first ones went into use on the island of Jersey in 1852.
checked: Hill sent Trollope to the Channel Islands; first Jersey pillar boxes in public use 23 November 1852; mainland Britain 1853.

text: Kazuo Ishiguro drafted nearly all of The Remains of the Day in about four weeks. He wrote freehand six days a week and let clumsy sentences stand so he could keep moving, then spent more time shaping it afterward.
checked: Ishiguro's own account: the four-week Crash, 9am to 10.30pm Monday through Saturday, wrote freehand, let awful sentences remain, more or less the entire novel down, then more time to write it up properly.

text: Zora Neale Hurston wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God in Haiti in about seven weeks. It came out in 1937, and decades later Alice Walker's 1975 essay helped bring it back to a wide audience.
checked: Background: written in Haiti in the span of seven weeks; published 1937; revival after Walker's 1975 Ms. essay.

text: N. K. Jemisin wrote her early novels while working as a mental health counselor. Reader support through Patreon let her quit that job in 2016, and she went on to win the Hugo for Best Novel three years in a row.
checked: Day job as mental health counselor; May 2016 Patreon funding let her quit; first to win Best Novel Hugo in three consecutive years.

text: Terry McMillan's first novel, Mama, grew out of a short story her writers group urged her to expand. When the publisher did little to promote it, she wrote to thousands of booksellers and set up her own readings, and the first printing sold out.
checked: Harlem Writers Guild encouraged expanding Mama; she wrote to thousands of booksellers, arranged her own tour; first 5,000 copies sold out.

text: J.K. Rowling got the idea for Harry Potter on a train trip in 1990. Her agent spent a year sending the book to publishers who passed before Bloomsbury took it, after the chief executive's eight-year-old daughter read it and loved it.
checked: Idea came on a 1990 train to London; second agent spent a year trying to sell it, most publishers thought it too long; Bloomsbury chief executive's eight-year-old daughter praised it.

text: Erin Morgenstern wrote The Night Circus over two rounds of National Novel Writing Month. The finished novel spent seven weeks on the New York Times bestseller list.
checked: Entry 1: The Night Circus written during two NaNos; seven weeks on NYT bestseller list.

text: Andy Weir posted The Martian a chapter at a time on his personal website while working as a programmer. When readers had trouble downloading it, he put it on Kindle for 99 cents, and soon an agent and a publisher called.
checked: Chapters posted on his site; free e-book; Kindle Direct at 99 cents; back at work as a programmer; then an agent called, then a publisher.

text: Hugh Howey was helping manage a bookstore when he self-published Wool as a short story. Sales took off, so he wrote four more stories, and together they became a full novel.
checked: Howey helped manage a bookstore; career took off with the short story Wool; sales rose quickly; he wrote four more stories that turned it into a full novel.

text: Beverly Jenkins started writing romance novels for fun while working at a reference desk, and she also worked in the Michigan State University library. Her first novel, Night Song, came out in 1994, and in 2017 she received a lifetime achievement award from Romance Writers of America.
checked: Began writing romance for fun while at Parke Davis reference desk in Ypsilanti; worked in MSU library circulation; Night Song, Avon, 1994; 2017 RWA Nora Roberts Lifetime Achievement Award.

text: Brit Bennett worked on her debut novel, The Mothers, for years. She wrote, rewrote and revised it starting back when she was in high school.
checked: Host introduction: she wrote and rewrote and revised the novel since she was in high school in Oceanside.

text: Alexander McCall Smith taught medical law at the University of Edinburgh and was around 50 when he was first published as a novelist for adults. He estimates he writes about 1,000 words an hour and now has more than 100 novels.
checked: Roughly 1,000 words every hour; taught medical law at Edinburgh; first adult novels around age 50; more than 100 novels.

text: Marissa Meyer's Cinder grew out of her 2008 National Novel Writing Month project. The idea came from a dream in which Cinderella was a cyborg who lost her foot at the ball instead of her shoe.
checked: Inspired by joining the 2008 NaNoWriMo contest; dream of cyborg Cinderella losing her foot; Cinder was her 2012 debut.

text: Sara Gruen wrote Water for Elephants as part of National Novel Writing Month. The novel spent 12 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list in 2006, later hit number one in paperback and became a film.
checked: Written as part of NaNoWriMo; 12 weeks on NYT list in 2006; paperback No. 1 in July 2007; 2011 film.

text: William Faulkner said he wrote As I Lay Dying in about six weeks while working nights at a power plant, writing from midnight to 4 a.m. on an overturned wheelbarrow he used as a table.
checked: Faulkner's own account: about six weeks, midnight to 4 a.m. at a Mississippi power plant, overturned wheelbarrow as a table.

text: After New York publishers passed on his first novel, E. Lynn Harris put out 5,500 copies of Invisible Life through his own small press and sold them from the trunk of his car at beauty salons, bookstores and book clubs. Once he had sold 10,000 copies, Doubleday signed him.
checked: Created his own Consortium Press; 5,500 copies printed December 1991; sold from car trunk at salons, bookstores, book clubs; Doubleday signed him after ten thousand copies.

text: John Grisham wrote his first novel, A Time to Kill, from 5 to 8 each morning while working as a lawyer and state legislator. The first printing was 5,000 copies, and he sold nearly 1,000 of them himself.
checked: Working from 5:00 to 8:00 each morning while practicing law and serving as legislator; 5,000-copy first printing, nearly 1,000 sold by Grisham.

text: Kathryn Stockett collected 60 rejection letters over three and a half years while trying to sell The Help. She kept working on the same story, and it became a bestseller and a hit film.
checked: 60 rejection letters over 3 and a half years; still working on the same story; bestselling book and successful movie.

text: Madeleine L'Engle nearly gave up writing on her 40th birthday. A Wrinkle in Time was rejected 26 times before Farrar, Straus and Giroux took it, and it won the Newbery Medal in 1963.
checked: 26 rejections before FSG; nearly gave up on her 40th birthday; won the 1963 Newbery.

text: Laura Ingalls Wilder was 65 when her first Little House book came out in 1932. Before that, in her 40s, she wrote for small farm publications in Mansfield, Missouri.
checked: Little House in the Big Woods published 1932 when Wilder was 65; wrote for small farming publications in Mansfield, Missouri in her 40s.

text: Raymond Chandler lost his oil company job during the Depression and began writing fiction at 44. He taught himself by studying and imitating a magazine story by Erle Stanley Gardner, and his first novel, The Big Sleep, came out in 1939.
checked: Dismissed from Dabney Oil in 1932; became a detective fiction writer at 44; imitated a Gardner novelette; The Big Sleep, 1939.

text: Colson Whitehead had the idea for The Underground Railroad in 2000 but waited years to write it. He said he felt he needed more maturity and a few more books behind him to do it justice.
checked: Idea in 2000, too scared to write it; needed more maturity and a few more books under his belt.

text: Tayari Jones wrote An American Marriage three full times before she settled on its structure of three narrators taking turns. She drafts on manual typewriters because they slow her down.
checked: Wrote the full novel three times before settling on three alternating narrators; says the typewriter slows her down.

text: Ann Patchett wrote her first novel, The Patron Saint of Liars, during a fellowship at the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown in her late twenties. It was published in 1992.
checked: Won a fellowship to the Fine Arts Work Center in her late twenties and wrote her first novel there; published 1992.

text: Frank McCourt spent years teaching in New York City schools before he published his first book. Angela's Ashes came out in 1996, when he was 66, and won the Pulitzer Prize the next year.
checked: Retired schoolteacher who taught in New York City schools; 66 when Angela's Ashes was published in 1996; Pulitzer in 1997.

text: For years Stephen King set himself a goal of 2,000 words a day, and later about 1,000. He keeps writing on holidays too, taking a short break only after he finishes a manuscript.
checked: Daily goal of 2,000 words for years, about 1,000 more recently; writes on holidays except 10 to 12 days off after finishing a manuscript.

text: James Baldwin wrote a play at 10 that impressed his teacher and published his first essay at 13. In 1951 he went off to a small village in the Swiss Alps to work on Go Tell It on the Mountain, which came out in 1953.
checked: Wrote a play at age 10; first essay at 13; retreated to a Swiss Alps village in 1951 to write the novel; published 1953.

text: Jack Kerouac filled journals with material for On the Road for years, then typed a draft on a single 120-foot scroll in 1951. He went on to rework it through as many as six drafts before it was published.
checked: Journals 1947 to 1949; 120-foot scroll; tinkered with up to six drafts from 1951 to 1957.

text: Facing a contract deadline in 1866, Fyodor Dostoevsky dictated The Gambler to a young stenographer, Anna Snitkina. With her help he finished on time, and Anna later became his wife.
checked: Deadline of 1 November 1866 under Stellovsky contract; dictated to Anna Snitkina; finished in time; she later became his wife. Age removed because sources differ (19 vs 20).

text: Mary Shelley was 18 when Lord Byron suggested a contest to write a frightening story during the summer of 1816. A waking dream gave her the idea for Frankenstein, which was published in 1818.
checked: 1816 near Lake Geneva; Byron suggested the contest; Mary was 18; waking dream; first published anonymously in 1818.

text: The Tale of Peter Rabbit began as an illustrated letter Beatrix Potter wrote to a young boy in 1893. Six publishers turned it down, so she paid to print 250 copies herself, and a publisher soon came back for a full-color edition.
checked: 1893 picture letter to Noel Moore; six publishers declined in 1900; private printing of 250 copies in December 1901; Warne edition October 1902.

text: Richard Adams worked as a civil servant and made up Watership Down to entertain his two daughters on long car rides. Seven publishers rejected the manuscript before it came out in 1972, when he was in his fifties.
checked: Story told on long car journeys to his daughters; civil servant career; seven publishers rejected it; published 1972 when he was in his fifties.

text: Roald Dahl wrote in his mother's old armchair with a board on his knees as a desk. He sharpened six pencils before starting, used yellow legal paper, and worked in two-hour sessions, one in the morning and one in the afternoon.
checked: Armchair belonged to his mother; baize-covered board on his knees; six Dixon Ticonderoga pencils; yellow legal paper; two two-hour sessions.

text: Louisa May Alcott was not eager when her editor asked for a book for girls, but she started Little Women in May 1868 and sent off the manuscript that July. Meg, Beth and Amy were based on her sisters, and Jo on herself.
checked: Thomas Niles asked for a girls' book; she was reluctant; began May 1868, sent manuscript July 15; characters based on her sisters and herself.

text: Ernest Hemingway wrote in the morning as soon after first light as he could. He liked to stop while he still knew what would happen next, so picking up the next day was easy, and he kept a chart of his daily word count.
checked: From his 1958 Paris Review interview: writes soon after first light, stops when he knows what happens next, charts daily output.

text: Jesmyn Ward searched for years for a publisher for her first novel and had decided to quit writing and enroll in nursing school when it was finally accepted. She later won the National Book Award for Fiction twice.
checked: Where the Line Bleeds accepted by Agate in 2008 just as she had decided to give up writing for nursing; NBA for Fiction in 2011 and 2017.

text: Chinua Achebe mailed his only handwritten copy of Things Fall Apart to a London typing agency and then heard nothing for months. He got one typed copy back, and the novel has since sold more than 20 million copies.
checked: Only handwritten copy sent to London typing agency; months of silence; one typed copy returned; more than 20 million copies sold.

text: Victor Hugo kept missing deadlines on The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, so he bought a new bottle of ink, put his clothes away in a wardrobe and settled in to work. He wrote a book of almost 200,000 words in about four and a half months.
checked: Missed deadlines; bought new ink and a woollen body-stocking, stored clothes in a wardrobe; almost 200,000 words in four and a half months.

text: Georges Simenon said in a 1955 interview that he never worked more than eleven days at a time on any of his books. He wrote in a focused stretch, allowed no interruptions, and published 76 Maigret novels.
checked: 1955 Paris Review claim of no more than eleven days at a time; isolated, uninterrupted work; 76 Maigrets published.

text: National Novel Writing Month began in July 1999 in the San Francisco Bay Area with just 21 participants. The next year it moved to November to make the most of the gloomy weather.
checked: History: Chris Baty started it in July 1999 with 21 participants; moved to November in 2000 to take advantage of the miserable weather.

text: The National Novel Writing Month goal of 50,000 words in November works out to about 1,667 words a day. In 2015 more than 430,000 people took part.
checked: 50,000 words by end of November, roughly 1,667 per day; 431,626 participants in 2015.

text: Hundreds of novels drafted during National Novel Writing Month went on to be published, including Water for Elephants, The Night Circus, Wool, Cinder and Fangirl.
checked: Nearly 400 NaNoWriMo novels traditionally published since 2006; examples listed include these five titles.

text: More than twenty publishers turned down Dune. It was finally accepted by Chilton, a company best known for car repair manuals, and went on to win both the Hugo and the Nebula.
checked: Over twenty publishers rejected it; Chilton specialized in car repair guides; won both the Hugo and the Nebula.

text: Ernest Hemingway said he rewrote the ending of A Farewell to Arms 39 times. His grandson later found 47 alternate endings among his papers.
checked: Hemingway told The Paris Review he rewrote the ending 39 times; Sean Hemingway found 47 alternate endings.

text: In On Writing, Stephen King offers a simple revision formula: the second draft equals the first draft minus 10 percent.
checked: Quotes the note King kept by his typewriter, as told in On Writing: 2nd Draft = 1st Draft minus 10%.

text: Jane Austen drafted Pride and Prejudice in her early twenties under the title First Impressions. A publisher turned it down by return of post in 1797, and it came out about 15 years later, in 1813.
checked: Drafted 1796 to 1797 as First Impressions; Cadell declined by return of post in 1797; published January 28, 1813.

text: After several publishers rejected Swann's Way, Marcel Proust had it published at his own expense in November 1913. It became the first volume of In Search of Lost Time.
checked: Rejected by Fasquelle, Ollendorff and the NRF; issued at the author's expense in November 1913; first part of In Search of Lost Time.

text: J.R.R. Tolkien was grading exam papers when he found a page a student had left blank. On it he wrote the first sentence of The Hobbit, years before the book came out in 1937.
checked: Marking exam scripts in the 1930s, Tolkien found a blank page and wrote the hobbit sentence on it; The Hobbit published autumn 1937.

text: Margaret Mitchell wrote the last chapter of Gone with the Wind first and the rest in no particular order. She kept nearly seventy chapters in manila envelopes, and the novel won the Pulitzer Prize in 1937.
checked: Wrote the last chapter first, others in no particular order; nearly seventy chapters in manila envelopes; Pulitzer 1937.

text: Freewriting, a method championed by Peter Elbow, means writing steadily without stopping to edit. Writing teachers also point out that you do not have to begin at the beginning; you can start with whatever section is ready.
checked: Remedies section: freewriting (Elbow), writing continuously without editing; no need to begin at the beginning; starting with a section other than the introduction.

text: The Pomodoro technique, often suggested for stuck writers, is simple: write for 25 minutes, then take a 5-minute break.
checked: Remedies section: working in pieces, such as Pomodoro, 25 minutes of writing then a 5-minute break.

text: Writer's Digest puts most novels somewhere above 55,000 words, with novellas at roughly 30,000 to 50,000. Short stories can run anywhere from 1,500 words up to about 30,000.
checked: Short stories 1,500 to 30,000; novellas about 30,000 to 50,000; novels 55,000 to 300,000.

text: According to one literary agent quoted by Writer's Digest, a first novel is easiest to sell at 80,000 to 100,000 words.
checked: Agent Lori Perkins: first-time novels easier to market at 80,000 to 100,000 words.

text: Christopher Paolini began Eragon as a teenager, and his family self-published it through their home-based company. He gave more than 135 talks at bookshops, libraries and schools before Knopf republished it in 2003.
checked: Started writing as a teen; self-published via Paolini International; over 135 talks on a year-long tour; Knopf edition August 26, 2003.

text: In the 1800s the German writer Gustav Freytag mapped dramatic structure as a pyramid with five parts: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.
checked: Freytag developed the pyramid in the 19th century; five elements listed as exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.

text: In the Poetics, Aristotle wrote that a complete plot has a beginning, a middle and an end. He defined each one simply by what comes before it and what follows it.
checked: Translation of Poetics 1450b to 1451a defining beginning, middle and end by what precedes and follows.

text: Joseph Campbell described the hero's journey, a pattern of departure, initiation and return, in his 1949 book The Hero with a Thousand Faces. George Lucas drew on it when making Star Wars.
checked: Published 1949; monomyth of departure, initiation and return; Lucas deliberately used it in Star Wars.

text: Christopher Vogler wrote a memo for Disney on using Campbell's hero's journey as a guide for scripts. He later expanded it into the book The Writer's Journey.
checked: Influence section: Vogler's Disney memo, later developed into The Writer's Journey: Mythic Structure for Writers.

text: Blake Snyder's Save the Cat came out in 2005. The title refers to the early scene where the hero does something that makes us want to root for them, and his beat sheet lists 15 key story beats.
checked: Book published 2005; Save the Cat names the scene where we meet the hero and like them; Beat Sheet with 15 beats.

text: Lisa Genova looked for an agent for over a year, then self-published Still Alice in 2007 and sold copies out of her car. An agent later sold it to Simon and Schuster, and it became a bestseller and an award-winning film.
checked: Tried to find an agent for over a year; self-published 2007; sold from her car; agent sold it at auction to Simon & Schuster; NYT bestseller and Oscar-winning film.

text: Charles Dickens's first novel, The Pickwick Papers, came out in 20 monthly parts from 1836 to 1837. Each part was a slim booklet in a blue paper cover.
checked: Published in twenty monthly numbers April 1836 to November 1837 in printed blue paper wrappers.

text: Ralph Ellison spent about seven years, from 1945 to 1952, writing his first novel, Invisible Man. It won the National Book Award for Fiction in 1953.
checked: Seven-year stretch 1945 to 1952; first-time author; National Book Award 1953.

text: J.R.R. Tolkien worked on The Lord of the Rings for about a dozen years, from 1937 to 1949, fitting it around his lectures and research as an Oxford don.
checked: Written over a dozen years beginning in 1937, completed 1949; Oxford don with little time of his own.

text: Randy Ingermanson's Snowflake Method starts with a single sentence about your story, then grows it into a paragraph, a page and finally a scene list. He notes a typical novel has around 100 scenes.
checked: Step one is a one-sentence summary; expands to paragraph, one-page and longer synopses, then scene list; typical novel around 100 scenes.

text: In a 1981 talk to the Ohio Arts Council, Toni Morrison said that if you find a book you really want to read and it does not exist yet, you must write it.
checked: Morrison's 1981 Ohio Arts Council remarks, reported by the Cincinnati Enquirer on September 27, 1981.

text: Toni Morrison was not the first with the idea. In an 1833 letter, Benjamin Disraeli recounted a dinner conversation where the same thought came up: when you want to read a book, write one.
checked: Disraeli letter to his sister Sarah, April 30, 1833, recounting a conversation in which the line about writing a book when you want to read one came up (framed via Dr Johnson).

text: National Novel Writing Month started a Young Writers Program in 2004 that let students set their own word goals. In its first year it reached 150 classrooms and about 4,000 students.
checked: Young Writers Program launched 2004 for K to 12; students set own goals; first year 150 classrooms and 4,000 students.

text: Getting stuck is nothing new. The term writer's block was first described clinically in 1947, and writers from Joseph Conrad to F. Scott Fitzgerald wrestled with it and still left us their books.
checked: Edmund Bergler described the condition in 1947; Fitzgerald and Conrad listed among writers who struggled with it.

text: Kurt Vonnegut wrote a master's thesis arguing that stories have shapes you can draw on graph paper. The University of Chicago rejected it, reportedly because it was simple and looked like too much fun.
checked: Thesis rejected because it was so simple and looked like too much fun; stories have shapes drawn on graph paper.

text: Gadsby, a 1939 novel by Ernest Vincent Wright, runs over 50,000 words without a single letter e. To keep himself honest, he tied down the e key on his typewriter.
checked: Over 50,000 words with no e; published 1939; disabled the e key by tying it down.

text: Georges Perec wrote a whole French novel, La Disparition, without the letter e. Its English translator managed to keep the same rule.
checked: Mentions Perec's La Disparition avoiding e and the English translation keeping the restriction.

text: Dr. Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham after his editor bet him $50 that he could not write a good children's book using only 50 different words. He did it, and the book came out in 1960.
checked: Bennett Cerf bet $50 that he could not write a book with only 50 distinct words; published August 12, 1960.

text: There is a prize for the oddest book title of the year. The very first winner, in 1978, was Proceedings of the Second International Workshop on Nude Mice.
checked: Diagram Prize first awarded 1978 to Proceedings of the Second International Workshop on Nude Mice.

text: The oddest book title prize for 2009 went to Crocheting Adventures with Hyperbolic Planes. One runner-up was What Kind of Bean Is This Chihuahua?
checked: Winner Crocheting Adventures With Hyperbolic Planes; runners-up include What Kind of Bean Is This Chihuahua?

text: The interrobang, a question mark and exclamation point squished into one mark, was dreamed up in 1962 by advertising man Martin Speckter. Bang was printers' slang for the exclamation point.
checked: Speckter, head of an ad agency, conceived it in 1962; name from interrogatio plus bang, printers' slang for the exclamation mark.

text: In 1968 some Remington typewriters came with an interrobang key, so typists could ask and shout at the same time.
checked: In 1968 some Remington typewriters had an interrobang key.

text: Japanese has a word, tsundoku, for buying books and letting them pile up unread. It blends a phrase for stacking things up for later with the word for reading.
checked: Defines tsundoku as buying books but never reading them; from tsunde-oku (pile up for later) and dokusho (reading books).

text: The earliest known printing of the word nerd is in Dr. Seuss's If I Ran the Zoo from 1950, where it is one of his made-up creatures.
checked: Leading theory: first appeared in print in If I Ran the Zoo (1950), listed among invented creatures.

text: In the early 1800s, schoolchildren finished reciting the alphabet with the & symbol, treating it almost like a 27th letter.
checked: Early-1800s schoolchildren ended their ABCs with the symbol, effectively the 27th member of the alphabet.

text: Children reciting the alphabet would end with and per se and, meaning and by itself. Said fast enough, it slurred into the word ampersand.
checked: Students said and per se and; over time the phrase was slurred into ampersand.

text: Charles Dickens had a secret door at his house disguised as a bookcase, covered in fake book spines. One joke title was The Life of a Cat, in nine volumes.
checked: Fact 1: secret bookcase door at Gad's Hill with fake spines including The Life of a Cat in 9 volumes.

text: In 2012 linguist David Crystal counted 252 words whose first recorded use in the Oxford English Dictionary came from Charles Dickens, including slow-coach and whoosh.
checked: David Crystal blog post, June 2012: 252 words with OED first recorded use in Dickens, including slow-coach (Pickwick, 1837) and whoosh (Letters, 1856). Butter-fingers removed because earlier uses have since been found.

text: About 50 cats live at Ernest Hemingway's old home in Key West, and roughly half have extra toes. Each one is named after a famous person, a tradition Hemingway started.
checked: About 50 cats, about half polydactyl; each named after a famous person, a practice Hemingway started.

text: Lewis Carroll invented chortle by mixing chuckle and snort, and galumph by mixing gallop and triumphant.
checked: Chortle, blend of chuckle and snort; galumph, blend of gallop and triumphant.

text: A portmanteau is a travel bag, and Lewis Carroll borrowed the word for blends like brunch and smog, where two words are packed into one.
checked: Carroll applied portmanteau, a travel bag, to blended words such as brunch, smog and spork.

text: The little dot on top of a lowercase i or j has a name: it is called a tittle.
checked: Lead: the tittle or superscript dot is the dot on top of lowercase i and j.

text: The phrase to a T may come from tittle. People said to a tittle long before to a T caught on.
checked: To a T is thought to come from tittle, since to a tittle was used long before.

text: Horace Walpole coined serendipity in a 1754 letter, inspired by a fairy tale about three princes of Serendip who kept making happy accidental discoveries. Serendip was an old Persian name for Sri Lanka.
checked: Walpole letter of 28 January 1754; The Three Princes of Serendip; Serendip an old Persian name for Sri Lanka.

text: As a young teen, Stephen King hung his rejection slips on a nail in his bedroom wall. By 14 the nail could not hold them, so he swapped in a spike and kept writing. At 16, editors started adding encouraging notes.
checked: Excerpt from On Writing: nail above record player, replaced by a spike at fourteen; at sixteen, encouraging handwritten notes such as one from Algis Budrys.

text: The Library of Congress is the largest library in the world, with more than 173 million items and about 838 miles of bookshelves.
checked: Record: Library of Congress, 173,731,463 items and approximately 838 miles of bookshelves as of November 2021.

text: The first Little Free Library was built in 2009 in Hudson, Wisconsin, by Todd Bol, using wood from his old garage door, as a tribute to his mother. By 2018 there were more than 75,000 of them in 88 countries.
checked: First library 2009 from old garage door wood, honoring his mother June; Hudson, Wisconsin; over 75,000 in 88 countries per 2018.

text: The word robot comes from a 1920 play by Karel Čapek. He first wanted to call his creations labori, but his brother Josef suggested roboti instead.
checked: Coined in 1920 play R.U.R.; Čapek first considered labori; brother Josef suggested the final name.

text: Guinness lists Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time as the longest novel, at an estimated 9,609,000 characters. Plenty of time to get comfortable.
checked: Record: A la recherche du temps perdu, estimated 9,609,000 characters.

text: For Roald Dahl's 100th birthday, the Oxford English Dictionary added words tied to his books, including scrumdiddlyumptious, human bean and Oompa Loompa.
checked: Six entries added for Dahl's centenary, including scrumdiddlyumptious, human bean and Oompa Loompa.

text: The first author we know by name is Enheduanna, a priestess and poet in the ancient city of Ur. She was the daughter of King Sargon, who lived around 2300 B.C.
checked: First author known by name connected to an existing text; high priestess at Ur; daughter of Sargon (about 2334 to 2279 B.C.).

text: The semicolon made its first known printed appearance in 1496, in a short book by Pietro Bembo printed in Venice by the Aldine Press.
checked: Bembo's De Aetna, February 1496, printed by the Aldine Press, credited with the first printed semicolon.

text: The same Venetian printer that gave us the printed semicolon also made the first italic type, and in 1501 it printed a Virgil that was the first book set in italic.
checked: Aldine Press first used italic in 1500; the 1501 Virgil was the first book printed in italic type.

text: Lorem ipsum, the fake Latin used as placeholder text, is a scrambled passage from Cicero. A Latin scholar, Richard McClintock, published the link to its source in 1994.
checked: Derived from De finibus 1.10.32 to 1.10.33; McClintock's explanation first published in 1994 in a letter to Before and After magazine.

text: Sea otters sometimes hold paws while they nap so they do not drift apart. Groups of them floating together are called rafts.
checked: Sea otters link paws so they don't drift apart while napping; groups called rafts.

text: Sea otters have little pouches of loose skin under their forelegs where they can tuck snacks or a favorite rock.
checked: Loose-skin pouches under forearms used to carry snacks or favorite rocks.

text: Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a Viking-age king who united Denmark and Norway. The logo combines the runes for his initials, H and B.
checked: Named after Harald Bluetooth Gormsson who united Norway and Denmark; logo combines Nordic runes for H and B.

text: Agatha Christie said she used to work out plots while soaking in an old-fashioned tub, lining its rim with apple cores. She also did her thinking on walks and while washing dishes.
checked: 1966 New York Times: plots in the tub, lining the rim with apple cores; also walking or washing up.

text: The most overdue library book on record was borrowed from a Cambridge college library around 1667 and returned in 1956, roughly 288 years late.
checked: Sidney Sussex College book borrowed 1667 to 1668, returned 16 January 1956, Guinness record for most overdue library book.

text: George Washington borrowed a book from the New York Society Library and never brought it back. In 2010, 221 years later, Mount Vernon staff replaced it with a copy of the same edition.
checked: The Law of Nations, New York Society Library, 221 years overdue, returned 20 May 2010; Mount Vernon offered a replacement copy of the same edition.

text: In 2021 a school library in Peterborough, England, got back a book called Manners Make a Difference, 32 years late, along with a sheepish apology note. The fine was waived.
checked: Manners Make A Difference returned to St John Fisher Catholic High School, April 2021, 32 years overdue, with an apology note; fine waived.

text: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. Its blood is blue because it uses copper, not iron, to carry oxygen.
checked: Three hearts; hemocyanin with copper makes the blood appear blue.

text: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms, not its head, so each arm can act a bit on its own. And the accepted plural is octopuses.
checked: Roughly two-thirds of neurons in the arms, allowing semi-independent action; octopuses is the generally accepted plural.

text: The Oxford comma, the comma before and in a list, gets its name from Oxford University Press, which made it house style. It is also called the Harvard comma.
checked: Called the Oxford comma because of Oxford University Press house style; also Harvard comma via Harvard University Press.

text: A missing comma once cost a Maine dairy $5 million. A state law's list had no serial comma, a court found it ambiguous, and the company settled with its delivery drivers over overtime pay.
checked: O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy: wording without serial comma ruled ambiguous; Oakhurst settled for $5 million.

text: The paragraph mark, called a pilcrow, began as a C for the Latin word for little head. Scribes left blank spaces for it to be added later in red ink, and sometimes it never got filled in.
checked: By the 12th century scribes used a C from capitulum; spaces left for rubricators who filled them in red; sometimes left empty.

text: Melvil Dewey was a college student working in the Amherst library when he came up with his system for shelving books. He reportedly worked it out during a long Sunday sermon.
checked: Junior at Amherst working in the library in 1873; reportedly reached his solution during a long Sunday sermon.

text: Mark Twain's Life on the Mississippi was the first book sent to a publisher as a typewritten manuscript. Twain did not type it himself; someone typed it from his handwritten pages.
checked: Background: first submitted to a publisher as a typewritten manuscript; Twain did not use the typewriter himself, a secretary typed from his manuscript.
